improvements: Make the signal flow and measurement conventions understandable so an engineer can interpret results rather than just see numbers.
Keep the page focused on setting up a run, inspecting its outcome, and comparing saved work; make running, stopped, and completed states unmistakable.

quality.criterion: The local interface has a calm, exact, instrument-like visual direction: high-contrast measurement readouts, deliberate offline typography, and restrained controls.
quality.verification: Open the served page in a modern desktop browser; inspect hierarchy, contrast, labelled controls, keyboard operation, reduced-motion behavior, and the browser console.

quality.criterion: Each wave demonstrates its promised working behavior, with sessions surviving a server restart and remaining accessible through the applicable interfaces.
quality.verification: Run the documented wave examples, restart the server, and inspect saved sessions using the page and CLI.

quality.criterion: Cancellation numbers are reproducible and interpretable, including their band boundaries and the calculation convention used.
quality.verification: Run known tone and fixed-filter cases, independently check the reported band attenuation, and compare identical runs for zero delta.

quality.criterion: The limiter bounds every reported output sample, and stopping an active run promptly records its actual processed length and stopped status.
quality.verification: Run a deliberately divergent case and inspect the output array and limited flag; stop a sufficiently long active run and inspect its persisted status and processed_samples.

quality.criterion: The documented local workflow works without audio hardware, network access, or third-party runtime packages.
quality.verification: Follow docs/try-it.md on the supplied Windows runtime with network access disabled, including a generated signal and a compatible WAV import.

scopeIn: Build Quiet Bench, a noise-cancelling test bench that runs on this PC with no audio hardware. Python 3.12 standard library plus Node 20 for the page checks; no third-party runtime packages, no network.

Generate a noise signal (tones, band noise) or import a WAV file; simulate the acoustic path from the noise source to the ear, run an adaptive canceller (LMS family), and report cancellation in each frequency band.

Every session is saved on a small local storage server (`python server.py --port PORT --data DIR`) with its settings and results. Its web page starts runs, browses saved sessions, reloads one and compares two. A command line (`python bench.py run|list|show|export`) does the same without the page.
A limiter must hold the output inside a safe level when the filter diverges, and a stop switch ends a run at once.

Build and show three waves: Wave 1: the thinnest thing that runs end to end, one tone through a fixed filter, saved and shown. Wave 2: the adaptive filter, attenuation per band, browse and reload. Wave 3: compare runs, limiter and stop switch, WAV import.
CLI contract: bench.py run --data DIR --settings JSON; list --data DIR; show ID --data DIR; export ID --data DIR. run/show emit session JSON; list emits an array; export emits CSV.

API contract: POST /api/runs with settings -> session (asynchronous allowed); GET /api/sessions -> array; GET /api/sessions/ID -> session; POST /api/runs/ID/stop; GET /api/compare?a=ID&b=ID -> array of bands with low, high, delta_db = b minus a.
WAV contract: signal = {kind: wav, path: absolute WAV path}; 16-bit mono, same sample rate.

Session contract: id, settings, status (running/completed/stopped), limited (boolean), processed_samples, bands [{low, high, attenuation_db}], desired/residual/output sample arrays (before cancellation, error, limited anti-noise). Preserve this JSON as wave-1 legacy input.

Page contract: Accessible labelled textarea[name=settings] (JSON), Start run button, [data-session-id=ID] saved session buttons, select[name=compare-a], select[name=compare-b], Compare button and [data-comparison] result. Show session id and band numbers. docs/try-it.md gives actual start/stop and CLI commands.
scopeOut: Audio hardware playback or real-world acoustic safety certification.
Accounts, network access, deployment, paid assets, and third-party runtime packages.
Additional analysis or scope changes not agreed with the user.
answer.understanding: A local, offline acoustic simulation and adaptive-cancellation workbench, delivered visibly in three waves, with trustworthy measurements and bounded simulated output.
users: An audio engineer trying ideas before buying hardware.
answer.why: The staged delivery is intentionally thin at first, but signal processing, durable shared sessions, interoperable CLI and API contracts, and observable stopping and limiting make the complete outcome a large piece of work.

areas.responsibility: Implement deterministic signal generation, acoustic simulation, cancellation, measurements, limiting and cooperative stopping.
Own the local server, CLI, run lifecycle and durable session storage.
Build the accessible local page and document and demonstrate each wave's offline workflow.

contracts.text: Wave 1: simulation.run(settings) returns a JSON-serializable object with limited, processed_samples, bands, desired, residual and output; it raises ValueError for invalid settings. The service supplies id, original settings and completed status. The supported Wave 1 settings are sample_rate, samples, signal {kind: 'tones', frequencies: [one frequency], amplitude}, path (FIR coefficients), filter: 'fixed', and fixed_filter (FIR coefficients). Generate x[n] = amplitude*sin(2*pi*frequency*n/sample_rate), with zero initial history; desired is path convolved causally with x, output is the negated fixed_filter convolution with x, and residual is desired + output. Return exactly samples values in each array, processed_samples = samples and limited = false. Return one band covering 0 through Nyquist, with attenuation_db = 10*log10(sum(desired²)/sum(residual²)); reject a case with zero energy in either sum in this wave. Later waves extend this interface for adaptive processing, band measurements, limiting and stopping.

Wave 1: serve the page and its assets from web/ on the same localhost origin. POST /api/runs accepts a settings JSON object and synchronously returns the saved completed session as JSON; GET /api/sessions returns a JSON array and GET /api/sessions/ID returns the saved session. Invalid settings return HTTP 400 with JSON {"error":"message"}; unknown IDs return 404 with the same error shape. A session contains id, settings, status, limited, processed_samples, bands, desired, residual and output as specified by simulation-run. The page submits the labelled settings textarea, shows errors, session ID and band numbers, and can reopen the saved session after restart. Later endpoint additions are specified by compare-stop.

Wave 1: python server.py --port PORT --data DIR starts the local server; python bench.py run --data DIR --settings JSON prints the completed session JSON, and python bench.py show ID --data DIR prints that same persisted session JSON. Both use the same data directory and session representation; completed runs survive server restart and can be read through either interface. Errors go to stderr with a nonzero exit status. Later waves add list and CSV export while preserving Wave 1 session JSON as readable legacy input.
Wave 2 agreement: define reproducible band boundaries, spectral energy and zero-energy conventions consistently across computation, persisted sessions and documentation.
Wave 3 agreement: asynchronous run status and prompt stop, plus band-aligned comparison with delta_db equal to B minus A.

decisions.choice: Use a synchronous fixed-filter run for the first end-to-end slice; introduce asynchronous lifecycle only when stop is implemented.
decisions.reason: It makes the first demonstration small without precluding the required later stop behavior.

decisions.choice: Use the same local session store for CLI and server, retaining the Wave 1 session JSON as readable legacy input.
decisions.reason: Saved work must survive restarts and remain accessible from both interfaces.

waves.goal: Show one generated tone through a fixed filter, saved and displayed through the page and CLI; restart the server and reopen it. This establishes the first slice of the cross-wave commitments.
Add tone and band-noise generation, LMS cancellation, interpretable per-band attenuation, and saved-session browsing and reload; demonstrate the documented cases and persistence.

Complete comparison, limiter, prompt stop, compatible WAV import, full CLI and page contracts, and the offline documented workflow; demonstrate bounded output, actual stopped length, comparison and restart recovery.

answer.why: Three disjoint owners can start from the Wave 1 simulation, HTTP and persistence agreements in parallel. Commitments spanning waves are assigned to the wave where their full promise is complete; earlier slices are explicit in the wave goals. Later shared agreements are intentionally deferred until their wave is next.
